title: Data Centers That Make Water From Waste Heat
one_liner: Containerized membrane-distillation skids that use a liquid-cooled data center's own warm return loop to turn cooling-tower blowdown or brackish well water into clean make-up water.
customer: Colo and AI-hosting operators in Texas, Arizona and Nevada facing water audits, plus immersion-cooled bitcoin and HPC hosts whose loops run hot. Operators buy or lease; fabs later.
problem: Data centers are the target of water regulation (Texas freeze and reporting crime, Australian standards, New York and Ohio actions), and cooling blowdown creates a discharge headache. Desalination was uneconomic because heat was expensive, but a data center produces heat it must remove anyway.
solution: Integrate membrane-distillation modules from an existing OEM with the site's warm loop (liquid-cooled racks now return water at roughly 45-65 C, my estimate). The skid concentrates blowdown and produces distillate for make-up water, cutting purchased water and discharge volume. Add a metering-and-ledger layer that produces a verified 'water-negative' claim. First product: a 10-50 m3/day skid.
why_now: A 2025 Chinese plant reported desal near $0.28/m3 using waste heat (not fully verified). Liquid cooling is spreading, and regulators and lenders now ask for verified water use.
revenue_model: $250-600k equipment sale per skid, or water-as-a-service at roughly $1.5-3/m3 plus O&M. Regulatory value (fewer permits, less discharge) is the closing argument.
non_obvious_insight: Membrane distillation lost to reverse osmosis because it needs large amounts of heat, and a data center offers abundant heat that must be removed, so its energy cost is effectively negative. The villain of the water story becomes the equipment that solves it.
first_30_days: Find three immersion-cooled mining or HPC hosts in Texas with 55-65 C loops. Partner with an MD module OEM for a 5 m3/day trial unit ($60-120k). Sign an LOI with a host for a 90-day pilot that shares data on kWh-thermal per m3, TDS and fouling.

title: Men's Repair Crews Funded by Aging-in-Place Budgets
one_liner: A membership club for men 25-45 who show up weekly to do minor home repairs for isolated older adults, led by a paid tradesperson and paid for by aging-in-place budgets.
customer: Payers are Medicare Advantage plans (home-safety supplemental benefits), Area Agencies on Aging, city aging-in-place funds and Medicaid home-modification programs, paying $400-900 per job. Members add about $30 a month in dues.
problem: Men reject talk-based loneliness solutions, and therapy framing fails them. Men's Sheds show that shoulder-to-shoulder tasks build belonging (97% of members in one survey said they have a place where they belong), but they run on charity money. Meanwhile older adults with unfixed stairs, missing grab bars and poor lighting fall, and licensed repair labor for small jobs is scarce and expensive.
solution: Crews of 8-10 men with one paid licensed lead. A 3-hour Saturday job (grab bars, rails, ramps, lighting, smoke alarms) followed by a shared meal. Rotating pairs do check-in visits. Software handles referral intake from care managers, photo scoping, materials, volunteer liability coverage, and payer invoicing with before/after proof and a fall-risk checklist.
why_now: Male loneliness is now a headline metric (WHO commission, Jun 2025) but products remain talk-based. Medicare Advantage plans are under margin pressure and favor cheap benefits with hard outcomes such as fall prevention. Programs modeled on CAPABLE (repairs plus clinician visits) have shown large drops in daily-living disability. Trades labor is short.
revenue_model: Per-job fees from payers ($400-900), member dues, and materials sponsorship from hardware retailers. Volunteer labor makes the gross margin work. Later: employer-sponsored membership.
non_obvious_insight: Men join for a task, not a talk, so give them a task that a payer already funds and cannot staff. The 'male loneliness' problem and the 'home-modification labor shortage' are the same market seen from two sides.
first_30_days: Partner with one Area Agency on Aging or a Rebuilding Together affiliate that already has a waitlist of households. Recruit 8 men via a local run club, climbing gym and Reddit. Hire a retired contractor as lead at about $40 an hour. Complete 4 pilot jobs at $350 each, document outcomes, and pitch two Medicare Advantage care-management teams with the first 20 jobs.

title: Import Compliance Desk for Hobby Brands
one_liner: Subscription compliance for small tabletop, designer-toy, card-accessory and collectible brands covering CPSC eFiling, product certificates, EU representative and tariff classification.
customer: Indie designer-toy studios, board-game and miniature publishers, Kickstarter creators and card-accessory brands importing from Asia or selling into the EU and UK, with $0.5M-$20M in revenue.
problem: CPSC electronic certificate filing for regulated imports became mandatory on 8 July 2026 (no value-based exemption; foreign-trade-zone entries follow 8 Jan 2027). The EU requires a responsible person for consumer products. De minimis ended in Aug 2025, so small parcels are dutiable. Hobby brands have no compliance staff, and blind-box and collectible toys straddle the children's-product line.
solution: Per-SKU compliance dossiers (accredited lab test-report management, certificate generation, filing data handed to brokers), classification lookups, an EU authorized-representative service, label review, and a landed-cost API for the brand's storefront.
why_now: eFiling is live, counterfeit-toy seizures show heightened customs attention, and crowdfunded creators are hitting duty surprises for the first time.
revenue_model: $199-999/month plus $150-500 per-SKU dossier fees and an EU representative fee.
non_obvious_insight: Hobby brands do not hire compliance, and backers forgive late delivery but not a customs seizure. Vertical-specific rulings (dice, sleeves, miniatures, plush) are reusable across every customer, which is what makes a generic compliance vendor less useful.
first_30_days: Sell a $299 eFiling readiness audit to 15 publishers via BoardGameGeek and Kickstarter creator communities. Partner with one customs broker and one accredited lab.

title: Through-the-Package Drug Verification Library
one_liner: A subscription spectral fingerprint library and scan-on-receipt workflow that lets pharmacies and wholesalers verify what is actually in a sealed vial or blister pack, using off-the-shelf handheld Raman/NIR devices.
customer: 503A/503B compounding pharmacies and telehealth GLP-1 dispensers receiving vials or API from overseas, secondary wholesalers and repackagers, hospital pharmacies, and med-spa distributors.
problem: ARPA-H states that drug-related morbidity and mortality cost $528 billion per year, that recalls affect the medication of over 150 million Americans each year, that 'most recalls only happen after patients are exposed', and that only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports, a process that takes weeks. Serialization under DSCSA tracks the box (package-level identifiers, 24-hour notification of illegitimate product), not the molecule inside it, so a convincing counterfeit or diluted vial passes every paperwork check.
solution: Do not build hardware. Rent or resell existing handheld Raman/NIR units, and build the proprietary part: a reference library of authentic and adulterated finished-dose spectra measured through blisters, vials and prefilled pens, plus a classifier and a chain-of-custody report (photo, lot number, spectrum, pass/fail/uncertain). Uncertain results route to a partner lab for confirmatory HPLC. The library improves with every scan.
why_now: ARPA-H's FASTPASS program (solicitation ARPA-H-SOL-26-160; solution summaries due September 21, 2026, full proposals November 10, 2026) is funding through-packaging sensing (TA1 SAMPLE) and analytics (TA2 DETECT), which signals that the sensing hardware and spectroscopy science are mature enough to commercialize. GLP-1 volume and compounding have widened the exposure of small dispensers who have no way to check incoming product.
revenue_model: $1 to $3 per scan (usage SaaS), $300 per month device rental, $150 to $400 per escalated lab confirmation, and $6k to $24k per year library license for wholesalers.
non_obvious_insight: DSCSA verifies labels and traceability, not contents, and ARPA-H itself says the gap is one 'no single agency, manufacturer, or current technology can close alone'. That leaves room for a private data product. The moat is the library of through-package spectra, not the scanner, and it compounds with every customer scan. Evidence: https://arpa-h.gov/explore-funding/programs/fastpass ($528B, 150M Americans, 'only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports', TA1 SAMPLE and TA2 DETECT) and https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-supply-chain-integrity/drug-supply-chain-security-act-dscsa (package-level identification and 24-hour illegitimate-product notification). Caveat: the ARPA-H page did not give product types or counterfeit prevalence, and the GLP-1 exposure is my inference from public FDA alerts.
first_30_days: Pick 10 high-volume SKUs (injectable GLP-1 vials and pens plus a few high-value generics). Buy authentic references, make in-house dilution and wrong-API samples with a partner lab, rent two handhelds, and collect spectra through the packaging. Offer 3 compounding pharmacies and 2 regional wholesalers a free 30-day pilot with scan-on-receipt. Convert to paid on a per-scan plan. Skip the FASTPASS proposal unless a university partner handles it.

title: Vacancy-Permit Kit for Half-Empty Offices
one_liner: A sensor and inspection package that keeps half-empty office buildings insurable and safe during the 12-36 months of limbo before resolution.
customer: Special servicers, receivers and owners of office buildings under roughly 31% occupancy or with dark floors, plus lender-placed insurance managers.
problem: Many standard commercial property forms treat a building as vacant unless about 31% of its area is leased and in use, and after 60 days of vacancy exclude vandalism, water damage, theft and glass while cutting other payouts (buildings under renovation are exempt). Meanwhile stagnant plumbing raises Legionella risk, HVAC is wasted, and squatters and fire watch add cost. About 15.7% of office CMBS is in special servicing, and resolutions take years.
solution: Flow and temperature sensors with automated flush valves, HVAC setback tied to the building system, AI door and intrusion cameras and documented monthly inspections. Packaged as evidence for a vacancy permit or protective-safeguards endorsement and as reporting to servicers, installed only on dark floors.
why_now: Distress is at record levels with long resolutions, property insurance is costly and restrictive, and IoT and video analytics are cheap.
revenue_model: $0.10-0.30 per sf per year subscription plus $1-3 per sf install, with referral fees from commercial insurance brokers.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is writing about conversion, but nobody services the limbo period where value leaks through insurance denials and stagnant water. A few dollars of sensors can be cheaper than one uninsured water loss.
first_30_days: Partner with two commercial brokers who place vacant-building coverage. Pilot at two receiver-owned buildings for about $5K each. Ask an insurer to accept the protocol in writing.

title: Critical-Error Benchmark for Legal Transcription AI
one_liner: An independent, reporter-built test suite that scores transcription AI on the errors that lose cases, such as dropped negatives, swapped numbers, wrong speaker and uh-huh versus huh-uh. Court and law-firm buyers pay for procurement reports, and vendors pay for certification.
customer: State court administrative offices and county courts running digital-recording or AI pilots. Large law firm innovation and procurement teams. Insurer litigation-management groups. The AI transcription vendors themselves, who buy a certification badge.
problem: Every vendor claims 95-99% accuracy, measured as word error rate on clean audio. That metric treats 'I did not see him' becoming 'I did see him' as one wrong word in six, no worse than a dropped 'the.' Reporters know the real failure points: negations, numbers (fifteen versus fifty), proper names, speaker attribution in crosstalk, uh-huh versus huh-uh, soft-spoken witnesses, and interpreted testimony. Court procurement officers and firm buyers have no independent comparison, so RFPs copy vendor claims.
solution: Build a hidden test set from staged mock depositions and hearings. Working reporters play scripted witnesses and attorneys, recorded in courtroom reverb, on Zoom, with masks, accents and interpreters. Each recording has certified steno ground truth and annotated critical-error spans. Publish a Critical Error Rate per hour with per-category scores. Release a free public subset and leaderboard for credibility. Charge for private bake-offs on a buyer's own audio, graded by reporters. Sell annual certification with re-testing whenever a vendor updates its model.
why_now: Shortages are pushing courts to adopt digital and AI reporting, and Texas, North Dakota and California have all moved on it in different ways. The federal proposal for new Rule 707 signals that courts want reliability standards for machine output. Vendors are consolidating (Verbit owns Veritext). State court technology offices are writing RFPs now with no independent yardstick.
revenue_model: $15,000-$40,000 per court or firm procurement evaluation. $25,000-$75,000 per year per vendor for certification and re-testing. $3,000-$8,000 per year for benchmark subscription reports to firms and insurers. Licensing test sets to vendors under strict separation from the certification arm.
non_obvious_insight: Accuracy is measured by the people selling it. The profession that produces legal ground truth for a living is the natural auditor. A dropped 'not' is the error class that ends careers in this field, and word error rate hides it as noise.
first_30_days: Hire 8 working reporters at $75-$100 per hour for weekend sessions. Produce 20 hours of staged audio and run 6 vendors. Publish a free 'Negation Error Report' that reporter associations will share. Email 15 state court technology officers and the National Center for State Courts. Offer each vendor a free re-test to start certification conversations.

title: Layoff Compliance Autopilot for Mid-Size HR
one_liner: Software plus expert review that generates every notice, filing and adverse-impact analysis a reduction-in-force needs, including a documented record of whether AI or restructuring drove each decision.
customer: HR and legal teams at 200-5,000-employee companies and the boutique employment law firms advising them pay $4-15k per event or $12-30k a year.
problem: RIF rules are fragmenting by state. New York's WARN form asks whether layoffs stem from AI or automation, New Jersey mandates severance, and OWBPA requires age disclosures for group terminations. Remote workforces span 20+ states. Mid-size firms rely on $500-an-hour outside counsel or spreadsheets while age-bias and AI-washing scrutiny (Mobley v. Workday) rises.
solution: Upload the roster and selection criteria. The tool maps each jurisdiction's rules, generates notices, separation agreements and OWBPA disclosures, runs adverse-impact statistics (age, race, sex, disability, leave) with remediation suggestions, and builds an AI-attribution record of task-level evidence for each decision. It includes a filing calendar and a lawyer-in-the-loop review queue.
why_now: Cuts are steady even though Challenger totals are down 41% year on year, AI is the leading cited reason, and NY added an AI checkbox in 2025. Age-discrimination class actions are live, and LLMs now make document generation cheap while lawyers still sign off.
revenue_model: Per-event fee ($4-15k), annual subscription, and revenue share with reselling law firms.
non_obvious_insight: The pain is not 'AI layoffs' but the compliance combinatorics of remote-first firms. The economic buyers (law firms and HR) either bill by the hour or bear the risk, and steady low-volume cuts mean repeated use.
first_30_days: Build a state-by-state rule matrix for the top 12 states plus federal rules. Sell $2,500 'RIF readiness packs' to 10 boutique employment firms. Run three live RIF events with friendly firms.

title: Heat-Health Desk for Medicare Advantage Plans
one_liner: Forecast-triggered outreach and cooling delivery for the heat-vulnerable members whose hospital bills the health plan pays.
customer: Medicare Advantage, D-SNP and Medicaid managed-care plans in the Southwest, Southeast and Pacific Northwest (supplemental-benefits and medical-director teams).
problem: Summer 2026 brought the hottest US July on record and a European heatwave with about 38,000 provisional deaths (secondary source). Heat waves drive ER visits and admissions among older, medicated, low-income members. Plans pay the downstream cost but do not know which members lack working cooling or live on top floors. Cooling supplemental benefits are underused.
solution: Risk-stratify members by housing type, utility arrears, medications that impair heat tolerance and prior heat visits. Trigger phone outreach ahead of forecast heat, deliver and install AC or fans through partners, run check-in calls on days 1-3, and help prevent utility shutoffs. Report avoided ER visits.
why_now: After the 2026 heat shock, plan medical directors are looking for concrete heat programs. Off-season (Oct-Feb) is when supplemental-benefit budgets get set.
revenue_model: Per targeted member per month in season, or per intervention, plus shared savings.
non_obvious_insight: The party that absorbs the cost of heat is the health plan, not the city. Heat is a claims-management problem and belongs in the plan's budget.
first_30_days: Use public hospital heat-visit data to build a cost-per-heat-day case. Pitch 5 regional plans for a 2,000-member pilot next season, and line up an AC-delivery and check-in vendor.

title: Unbundling Edits for Pet Insurance Claims
one_liner: Give pet insurers the claim-edit engine human health has had for 30 years: canonical procedure codes, bundling rules, and price benchmarks for messy vet invoices.
customer: Pet insurance MGAs, carriers and TPAs adjudicating roughly 100k to 2M claims a year, the mid-size players without in-house claims data science. Later, corporate veterinary groups and pet-owner pre-treatment estimate checks.
problem: Veterinary invoices are free-text line items exported from practice-management systems, with no universal procedure code set and no NCCI-style edits. Adjusters hand-review them. Insurers cannot tell that the vet billed anesthesia monitoring, an IV catheter, fluids and the e-collar as separate lines on top of a surgery fee, or what a routine dental cleaning costs in a given ZIP code. Claim severity is inflating with vet consolidation, and insurers answer with blanket premium hikes instead of line-level accuracy.
solution: An API that ingests invoice PDFs or line items. An LLM plus a hand-built taxonomy of the top ~300 vet procedures (about 80% of spend) normalizes each line to a canonical code. A rules layer, built the way NCCI and medically-unlikely edits work, flags unbundling, duplicates and implausible units. A benchmark layer returns usual-and-customary ranges by ZIP and practice type. The adjuster sees pay, reduce or review, with reason codes.
why_now: There are roughly 7 million insured US pets, and the segment is growing at double-digit rates with loss-ratio and price-hike pressure. Corporate vet consolidation is raising invoice complexity. LLMs make invoice line-item normalization, the hard part that took human-health edit vendors years, cheap enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: Per-claim fee of $0.25-$0.75, or 10-15% of validated savings. A 500k-claim MGA is worth $150-350k a year. Add a benchmark-data license for vet chains and an owner-facing estimate checker later.
non_obvious_insight: Every automation wave in healthcare billing started with standardized codes and claim edits, not with AI. Cotiviti and Optum are basically edit libraries with sales teams. Pet insurance is at the pre-CPT stage. Someone who has spent years living inside code sets, bundling logic and 'this is included in the global fee' arguments can build the missing layer in weeks. Insurers will not fund a fight with vets. They will fund a neutral, consistent, explainable edit that does not vary by adjuster.
first_30_days: Recruit one ex-coder (CPC) and a vet tech consultant. Build the 300-line taxonomy from public estimate sheets and a few hundred sample invoices. Approach 10 pet-insurance MGAs and TPAs with a free retrospective: run 5,000 of their anonymized past invoices and report the dollar share found in bundled, duplicate or out-of-range lines. Convert the best result into a paid pilot on per-claim pricing.

title: Parametric Insurance on Colorado River Shortage
one_liner: Insurance and hedges that pay out when official Colorado River operating triggers or reservoir projections cross agreed thresholds, sold to large industrial and municipal water buyers.
customer: Chip fabs, data centers, breweries, resorts, master-planned developers and municipal utilities that depend on Lower Basin supplies. Buyers pay premiums, and reinsurance and capital-markets funds take the risk.
problem: Powell plus Mead storage is about 36% and 95% of the basin is in drought. About $1.4T of annual activity is exposed, yet businesses cannot hedge water-supply or rate shocks except by capex. Until this year the rules were too ambiguous to write a contract against.
solution: Start with a Lower Basin water-supply risk index and term sheets, sold to muni-bond investors and industrial water buyers. Then build a parametric product that pays on published operating triggers or reservoir projections, funded through a surplus-lines or Lloyd's partner with an experienced weather-risk insurer. Payouts fund contingency supply, recycling or trucked water.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Record of Decision set the 2027-2036 operating framework, converting political ambiguity into published rules that a contract can reference. Capital-markets investors seek risks uncorrelated with catastrophe.
revenue_model: Premium (a percentage of limit), analytics licensing before any policy is issued, and a share of fund fees.
non_obvious_insight: The ROD makes the river's rules legible, which is the precondition for a derivative. The correlated hydrology scares traditional insurers, but that is exactly what non-catastrophe capital wants to hold.
first_30_days: Build the risk index from Reclamation's public 24-Month Study projections and reservoir data. Interview 10 fab, data-center and utility water managers on what loss they fear. Approach one weather-risk reinsurer and one ILS fund. First revenue comes from analytics sold to bond funds and industrial users.

title: Refundable Deposits Against AI Submission Floods
one_liner: A gateway that makes AI-generated reports, applications and pitches post a small refundable stake, so maintainers only read submissions someone bet on.
customer: Open-source maintainers and foundations, bug-bounty program owners, and other inboxes overwhelmed by AI-generated submissions (journals, grant makers, VC and press inboxes, public-comment portals). Start with OSS security teams and mid-size bounty programs.
problem: curl scrapped its bug bounty in January 2026 after valid reports fell below 5%, and its maintainer floated an entrance fee. HackerOne reportedly paused its Internet Bug Bounty in March after a 76% year-on-year jump in submissions, and other projects have retired bounties. Agents removed the effort-based backpressure open-source governance relied on. Content classifiers lose the arms race to models that write plausible reports.
solution: A stake API and form: the submitter (human or agent) posts a refundable deposit of $5-$50 by card or machine payment. Triage marks the report valid (refund plus any bounty) or invalid (deposit goes to maintainers or charity). Integrations for GitHub Security Advisories, email intake and bounty-platform webhooks. Reporters with track records get deposit discounts, and unpaid stakes flow to the program.
why_now: The curl and HackerOne events are recent and public. Machine Payments Protocol (March 2026) and card rails make small, programmatic deposits practical, and agents now file at scale.
revenue_model: 10-15% of forfeited deposits plus $99-$499/month per program for triage tooling, with sponsor-funded tiers for open-source projects.
non_obvious_insight: Price is the only filter that scales with attacker capacity. An agent must risk money on every claim, honest reporters get refunded, so the cost lands only on slop. Postage as a spam filter failed when senders were humans, but agent-operated senders have budgets and ROI math.
first_30_days: Build a GitHub Security Advisory plus web-form integration in two weeks. Recruit 5 OSS projects that have publicly complained and run a 30-day pilot measuring valid-report rate. Then approach bounty platforms with the data.

title: Dog Walkers as Repeat-Pass Sidewalk Inspectors
one_liner: Pay dog walkers a few dollars a day to mount a phone on their chest and sell the resulting block-by-block sidewalk condition layer to cities, utilities, and delivery-robot operators.
customer: City public works and ADA coordinators (mid-size cities of 100k to 500k people first), plus fiber and utility contractors and sidewalk delivery-robot operators as second buyers. Walkers are the paid supply side.
problem: Cities are legally on the hook to inventory sidewalks and curb ramps and fix trip hazards. Today that means an expensive contractor van or LiDAR survey every 5 to 10 years, or 311 complaints that skew toward loud, wealthy neighborhoods. Residential side streets go stale, and nobody sees a slab heave, a missing curb ramp, or a new obstruction until someone sues or gets hurt.
solution: A harness or chest mount plus a background app that runs during walks. It records geotagged video, and an on-device model flags heaved slabs, missing or noncompliant curb ramps, obstructions, standing water, and broken glass. Faces and plates are blurred on the phone and nothing is recorded near windows or interiors. Walkers earn per validated mile (roughly $1 a mile, so about $8 to $15 a day for something they already do). The city gets a rolling map with change detection, exported to its existing GIS or asset-management tools. A free 'dog hazard' layer (glass, bait or poison reports, hot pavement, off-leash aggressive dogs) gives walkers and owners a reason to adopt it. I have not verified current competitors or municipal pricing, so both should be checked before the pitch.
why_now: In 2026 a phone can run a decent defect-detection model offline, which was not practical a few years ago. Cities face ongoing ADA sidewalk obligations and litigation risk with tight budgets, which favors cheap continuous data over big one-off surveys. Driver-sourced street imagery (Hivemapper and Nexar style) has proven that crowds get paid for mapping, but the pedestrian tier is essentially unclaimed.
revenue_model: Annual municipal data subscription, or per-mile survey pricing that undercuts contractor quotes, at roughly $20k to $150k a year per city. Secondary sales of the same data to utilities, telecom build QA, and robot-delivery mapping. Walkers are paid about 30 to 40 percent of revenue as per-mile payouts.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody walks a residential sidewalk more than a dog walker: the same 3 to 5 miles, five days a week, at a slow pace, with eyes on the ground because dogs eat everything. The scarce asset in infrastructure data is not coverage, it is repeat passes, which is what makes change detection possible. That is exactly what a walker's fixed route produces for free.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 to 20 walkers through local pet-sitter Facebook groups and Nextdoor, since they are already clustered by neighborhood. Build the capture app with a cheap phone mount and an open sidewalk-defect model fine-tuned on public sidewalk datasets. Map about 200 miles of one neighborhood, then take a before-and-after sample to a city ADA or transportation coordinator. Offer a free neighborhood pilot with a cost comparison against contractor rates, and aim for a small pilot purchase order under the city's simple-purchase threshold.

title: Restaurant Kitchens as Chefs for Small Care Homes
one_liner: License a turnkey program that lets restaurants use dead hours to cook dietitian-approved, texture-modified meals for 6-20 bed assisted-living and adult-family homes that big foodservice ignores.
customer: Operators of small licensed residential care homes (adult family homes, board-and-care, personal care homes, small RCFEs) pay per resident per day, typically $8-12 for lunch and dinner. Adult children pay for premium 'chef-cooked' upgrades. The restaurant is the supplier, and the platform takes a license fee and revenue share.
problem: In a small care home, food is the main daily pleasure and the top resident complaint, yet it is cooked by overworked caregivers from warehouse-club and broadline food, with little variety and hard-to-manage special diets (mechanical soft, pureed, low-sodium, diabetic). Sodexo and Compass do not serve 6-bed homes and meals-on-wheels serves people at home. Meanwhile my kitchens sit idle from 2 to 5pm and on slow days, my cooks want more hours, and my dine-in traffic is soft.
solution: A meal program in a box for restaurants: a rotating 5-week menu library with dietitian sign-off and texture-modified variants (IDDSI levels), allergen and diet labels, batch-cook and cook-chill (or same-day hot delivery) SOPs, a state-specific health-department pre-clearance checklist and HACCP plan templates, routing and billing software, and a contracted registered dietitian on retainer. The restaurant cooks in dead hours and delivers 2-3 times a week in labeled pans, and the care home reheats. Ten homes at about $17-22k per year each is $170-220k of found revenue at healthy contribution margin on capacity that was previously idle.
why_now: The 65+ population is growing fast (the 'Peak 65' wave runs through about 2027). Families are shifting to small, cheaper residential homes rather than large assisted-living campuses. Restaurant dine-in traffic has been soft and owners are actively looking for non-traffic revenue. Kitchen labor is short, and steady off-peak hours help retention. Public state license lists make the small-home buyer easy to find. I couldn't verify current home counts this session, so pull the licensing-list counts state by state before building.
revenue_model: Onboarding fee of $1-2k per restaurant, plus 10-15% of meal revenue, plus software billing at about $100 per month per restaurant. Optional premium tier for adult-child paid 'chef upgrades' and dietitian services.
non_obvious_insight: The gold is in the mismatch between an idle asset and an ignored customer. Small-home operators are often immigrant nurses and caregivers running a tiny business with no procurement power, and no large foodservice company will serve them, but a two-location restaurant can absorb a 300-meal-per-week route into dead hours at nearly zero marginal labor cost. What a restaurant cannot do alone is the compliance layer (texture modification, diet labeling, dietitian review, regulator pre-clearance), and that is the product.
first_30_days: Pull the state's public list of small residential care homes and shortlist 30 within a 15-minute drive. Call my health department to confirm what is required to supply prepared meals from a licensed restaurant to a licensed facility. Hire a freelance registered dietitian by the hour for one 2-week menu. Offer 3 homes a free trial week, then convert them at about $9 per resident per day. Document the SOPs and the regulator's answer as the first version of the product.

title: Closing Ceremonies for Layoffs and Team Sunsets
one_liner: Trained ex-chaplains and celebrants who design and run dignified endings for teams hit by AI-driven layoffs, project sunsets and site closures.
customer: HR and people leaders at mid-size and large firms (500-5,000 employees) restructuring around AI, and outplacement firms that want to bundle a meaning-making service.
problem: Challenger reports AI was cited in about 112,713 announced US job cuts through July 2026 (about 24% of all cuts) and has led all reasons for five straight months. Layoffs are still delivered in a 15-minute video call and followed by résumé workshops. Nobody marks what ended, so leavers feel discarded, survivors feel guilty and disengage, and the company inherits hostile alumni.
solution: A 'Closing' package after legal communications are done: a facilitated last-day ceremony with a witness circle, a symbolic hand-off of work, a leaver-alumni charter (references, introductions), a manager script that bans corporate euphemism, and a survivor circle a week later. It is delivered in person or on video by a trained celebrant or ex-chaplain.
why_now: AI-attributed layoffs have become the leading cause of job cuts in 2026, and waves are recurring. Employer brand and alumni networks now matter for boomerang hiring and recruiting, and workers are openly sceptical of 'AI restructuring' messaging.
revenue_model: $4-12k per event, annual retainers of roughly $30-100k for an 'endings desk' that supports repeated restructurings, per-seat training licences for managers, and channel fees from outplacement partners.
non_obvious_insight: Companies overspend on what people do next and underspend on acknowledging what just ended. A layoff is a funeral without a ritual, and the missing ritual is the root of downstream problems: regretted attrition, employer-brand damage and lost referrals. A ceremony costs a tiny fraction of severance and is the only lever that changes how people talk about the company afterwards.
first_30_days: Recruit three ex-chaplains or celebrants. Build a 2-hour and a half-day format with a legal-review partner. Approach 15 outplacement consultants and 30 people-operations leaders, and offer one discounted team pilot in exchange for a case study.

title: Immigration Deadline Sentinel for Work-Permit Households
one_liner: The wealthy keep immigration counsel on retainer to calendar, file early and bridge gaps; for $20/mo, give H-4, OPT, asylum-applicant and DACA households an encrypted deadline vault and family-readiness plan.
customer: Households whose work authorization depends on renewable USCIS documents: H-4/L-2 spouses with EADs, F-1 OPT/STEM OPT students, asylum applicants, DACA recipients, and pending adjustment applicants. Sold at $20/mo per household, or $4-8 per head through employers, university international offices, credit unions and churches.
problem: DHS ended automatic 540-day EAD extensions for renewals filed on or after 30 October 2025. USCIS advises filing up to 180 days early, yet some I-765 categories are reported at many months to a year or more, so gaps in work authorization mean lost jobs, licenses and health coverage. Rich families' lawyers prevent this by tracking every date; ordinary families rely on memory and WhatsApp.
solution: An end-to-end-encrypted vault, on-device where possible: photograph an EAD, I-94 or I-797 and it extracts dates and builds a household calendar (EAD file window opening at day 180, AR-11 address change within 10 days, OPT unemployment day counter, I-751, N-400 windows, passport expiries). It pre-fills renewal packets for attorney review, generates employer bridging letters, and monitors case status. For cases outside normal processing times it prepares a congressional-inquiry package. It adds a family-readiness plan (power of attorney, standby guardianship for children, contact tree, know-your-rights card). Flat-fee referrals go to attorneys and DOJ-accredited representatives. It is software and documents, not legal advice.
why_now: The October 2025 interim final rule ended automatic extensions, processing times are long, USCIS moved to a new I-765 form version (mandatory from March 2026), and enforcement anxiety is high in 2026. Employers and universities are scrambling to protect workers.
revenue_model: $20/mo per household; $3-6 per employee per month for employer or university dashboards; flat referral fees from partner attorneys; enterprise HR reporting tier.
non_obvious_insight: Wealthy people's immigration counsel adds most of its value before a crisis, by calendaring, filing early and pre-drafting backups, which software can supply for a fraction of the cost. Privacy-by-design (end-to-end encryption so a subpoena or breach yields nothing) is not just compliance but the differentiator for a population that fears data exposure. The paying wedge is the professional H-4/OPT segment and their employers, not the most vulnerable households.
first_30_days: Build a WhatsApp and spreadsheet MVP that ingests document photos and sends reminders. Partner with 2 immigration attorneys on flat-fee referral, 3 university international offices, and H-4 spouse and OPT Facebook groups. Enroll 100 households free, convert to $20/mo, and pilot with one employer HR team.

title: Hazmat Sidecar for Small Old-House Repairs
one_liner: A flat-price, same-week asbestos and lead test-and-remove service that solo-to-five-tech plumbing, HVAC, electrical and flooring shops call when a small job in a pre-1980 house hits suspect material, with the waste manifest handled for them.
customer: Small trade shops (pay per call and pass through) and homeowners; property managers are a later segment.
problem: Median home age is 44 years and 62% of homeowners now choose repair over replace, so small jobs constantly disturb duct wrap, vinyl tile, transite, plaster and lead paint. Licensed abatement firms impose $2-5K minimums and weeks of lead time, so contractors either walk away (feeding the 73% project backlog) or cut corners and carry liability. Few landfills accept asbestos waste, and manifests and pre-notification confuse small shops.
solution: A van with two accredited techs: same-week sample results through a partner lab, flat-fee minor removal where state rules allow (subcontracted where they don't), bagged, labeled and manifested disposal, and a digital clearance letter the trade can hand the homeowner. Shops book by text and can subscribe for priority.
why_now: Repair-over-replace, tariff-inflated equipment and HVAC's 2025 shipment trough leave small shops chasing any billable job and unwilling to lose one to a hazmat surprise. Larger platforms (ServiceTitan, PE roll-ups) do not serve sub-$10K jobs.
revenue_model: $300-1,500 per job; per-sample testing fees; $99/mo priority subscription for trade shops.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not removal labor but the disposal chain: manifests, landfill acceptance and pollution insurance. Owning that chain lets one small team become the referral default for every trade in the area.
first_30_days: Days 1-30: complete state inspector accreditation, lead-safe firm certification and worker courses, get a pollution-liability quote and sign a landfill acceptance agreement. Meanwhile pre-sign 10 trade shops to a flat-price menu. Days 30-90: run the first 20 jobs and refine pricing.

title: Deferred-Payment Shield for Grain Sellers
one_liner: A counterparty-risk monitor plus surety/letter-of-credit wrap that turns the unsecured December 'deferred payment' loans farmers unknowingly make to their elevators into protected receivables.
customer: Row-crop operators with 2,000+ acres who each defer $400k to $2M of grain revenue into January, and the ag lenders and farm CPAs who advise them. Co-ops and elevators with strong balance sheets are a secondary payer, because the wrap becomes a way to win bushels.
problem: Every November and December, farmers sign deferred payment contracts to push income into next year for tax reasons. Most think they are just delaying a check. Legally, title has passed and they are unsecured creditors of the buyer. Iowa's Grain Indemnity Fund gives deferred payment contracts zero coverage. Deferred pricing ('price later') contracts get 75% coverage capped at $400,000 per claimant. Farm balance sheets are stretched, so more farmers are lending large sums to buyers they have never vetted.
solution: Start with a free 'Elevator Exposure Report'. The farmer lists every open contract, prepaid input balance and stored-grain receipt. The tool compares total exposure with the Fund's actual coverage and scores each buyer using licensing status, audit history, buyer size, and settlement-timing behavior reported by users. Then sell the fix. A specialty MGA or bank issues a surety bond or standby letter of credit against the buyer's payment promise, structured with ag tax counsel so tax deferral is preserved. The fee is roughly 0.3% to 0.8% of face value. Ag lenders subscribe to a portfolio dashboard showing how much of their borrowers' grain receivables sit with weak buyers.
why_now: Chapter 12 farm bankruptcies rose 46% in 2025 and April 2026 hit a six-year high. USDA projects record farm debt of about $625B in 2026. The 2025 bumper crop and low prices pushed farmers toward deferral and storage. The 2026 December deferral season opens in about 90 days, which is a hard deadline for a first pilot.
revenue_model: Wrap fee split with the surety or LC provider (0.3% to 0.8% of contract face value). Ag lender portfolio-monitoring subscription ($1k to $5k a month per lender). Optional $299 per farm annual exposure audit sold through CPAs.
non_obvious_insight: The elevator that pushes deferred payment contracts hardest in November is often the one that needs your cash, because deferrals are free working capital for a thinly capitalized buyer. Farmers think of the elevator as a warehouse. Once title passes, it is a borrower. Nobody rates that borrower.
first_30_days: Build the exposure calculator as a free web form and scorecard from Iowa Dept. of Ag license data and public filings. Get 5 farm CPAs and 3 rural banks to run their biggest clients through it. Sign one surety broker or bank willing to quote wraps, and target 10 paid wraps before the December deferral rush.

title: Medicaid Exemption Evidence Packs for FQHCs
one_liner: An EHR-connected engine that packages state-accepted exemption evidence (medically frail, SUD treatment, disability) so providers keep patients enrolled.
customer: FQHCs, safety-net hospitals and Medicaid MCOs in the 41 expansion states.
problem: Work requirements start Jan 1, 2027 (80 hours a month). Self-attestation is allowed only in 2027 and documentation tightens Jan 1, 2028, with 5.5-6.3M projected coverage losses and a 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hit for hospitals in expansion states. Clinical exemption evidence sits in provider EHRs but nobody packages it for state portals.
solution: Identify likely-exempt patients from problem lists and encounters, generate state-specific attestation and documentation packets, track renewal and verification dates, and give financial counselors a dashboard and patient outreach texts. Wedge is the clinical side, not the state's income-and-hours verification.
why_now: The CMS final rule and state notice deadlines (Aug 31, 2026) are done and system build is underway, so providers have about 3 months of runway. Patient-facing startups exist, but provider-side exemption evidence is mostly open.
revenue_model: $3-8 per covered high-risk member per month, or $75-150 success fee per retained member (an FQHC visit under PPS pays far more than a sliding-fee uninsured visit).
non_obvious_insight: States and their vendors handle income and hours data. The medically-frail and treatment-participation evidence lives with providers, and each retained Medicaid patient is worth many times the fee.
first_30_days: Sign 3 FQHCs in one state through the primary-care association. Manually pull 500 patients' problem lists and produce exemption packets. Measure approval rates, then automate state by state.

title: Add Megawatt-Hours to Already-Interconnected Batteries
one_liner: The queue limits megawatts, not megawatt-hours, so sell cheap add-on energy blocks to existing 2-hour battery and solar sites that already own the grid connection.
customer: Owners of 2019-2024 vintage 2-hour storage and solar sites (IPPs, infrastructure funds, utilities) in PJM, ERCOT and CAISO. Storage developers and data center developers who lack queue positions are the second buyer group.
problem: New MW wait years in interconnection queues. Stationary packs fell 45% to about $70/kWh and new projects average 3.5 hours. Existing 2-hour fleets are under-accredited for capacity, and their owners are not thinking about bolt-on energy.
solution: Engineer and finance duration uplift by adding DC-coupled or AC-block MWh behind the existing inverters and point of interconnection. Provide standardized BMS integration and warranty tooling. Second product: use surplus interconnection headroom at solar and wind farms to add storage MW, with a revenue share to the site owner. The company screens sites from public data, packages them and sells them or builds them.
why_now: Cell prices collapsed. Capacity prices at the cap reward accredited duration. Regulators (surplus interconnection service, MISO ERAS, PJM RRI) are openly trying to reuse existing grid connections.
revenue_model: Engineering and development fee per kWh added, a share of incremental capacity revenue, or resale of ready-to-build projects.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is the interconnection agreement, not the battery. Every existing 2-hour battery is a queue position with half its energy potential unused, and it is the one capacity addition that skips the queue.
first_30_days: List ~200 US storage projects at 2 hours or less from EIA-860 and ISO data. Model uplift economics for 10 of them under PJM and ERCOT rules. Send owners a one-page 'what two more hours earns you' analysis. Sign two or three paid feasibility studies. Line up a non-FEOC DC block supplier.

title: Pay-Per-Decibel Neighbor Trust for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent trust that owns a sensor mesh around a data center and automatically pays nearby households every time the hum exceeds agreed limits, turning 'trust us' into a self-executing contract.
customer: Data center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams, their land-use counsel, and counties negotiating community benefit agreements. Pre-application projects facing a rezoning fight are the entry point.
problem: Local opposition blocked or delayed roughly $130B of US data center projects in 2026, and opposition groups more than doubled to 833 by March. Developers' flat checks get called bribes: a $10,000-per-household offer to 4,500 households was rejected by residents in September. Noise promises are unenforceable, and dBA ordinances miss the low-frequency hum residents complain about. Counties lack staff to monitor compliance.
solution: A neighbor trust, funded by a developer bond, with three parts. (1) Trust-owned acoustic, low-frequency and vibration sensors, publicly viewable in real time. (2) A pre-agreed parametric schedule: any household within the radius gets an automatic payment for each night the level exceeds the threshold, so the payout works like a warranty on quiet. (3) Escalation funding for window and HVAC retrofits if exceedances persist. The trust also reports compliance to the county, giving regulators enforcement without new staff.
why_now: Opposition is peaking (about 120 projects stalled in H1 2026, more than 300 state bills, moratoria such as New York's), and developers are now experimenting with direct household payments and getting burned on credibility. Developers now need a neutral administrator, and no obvious specialist exists.
revenue_model: Developer pays $150k to $500k setup per campus, plus 8% to 12% of the annual fund as administration, plus sensor-as-a-service fees. Add county compliance-monitoring contracts. A single multi-billion-dollar campus can absorb this as a rounding error against months of delay.
non_obvious_insight: Neighbors rarely reject data centers over money. They reject unmeasured, unpriced harm. Making the harm measured and self-paying changes the negotiation and gives the developer a real financial reason to buy quieter chillers and dampers. The low-frequency, night-time signature is what the trust measures, and ordinances miss it.
first_30_days: List the next five county hearings on data center rezoning from local news and Data Center Watch. Hire a freelance acoustic engineer and build a $2k-per-node sensor kit from off-the-shelf parts. Offer a free 60-day neutral baseline noise map to one pending project, in front of both the developer and the opposition group. Convert that goodwill into a paid pre-application baseline of $50k to $100k and an MOU for the trust structure.

title: Farmer-Photo Crop Insurance Verification
one_liner: Replace satellite guesswork with dense, fraud-checked farmer photos, read by locally trained crop models, to trigger insurance payouts.
customer: Agricultural insurers and reinsurers, agri-input companies and cooperatives in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.
problem: Western models fail spectacularly on African crops, index insurance has high basis risk, and manual claim verification costs more than a smallholder premium.
solution: A local crop-damage model trained on image datasets (one project has 5M+ crop images) that takes geo-tagged WhatsApp photos, cross-checks neighbouring farms and weather, and triggers mobile-money payouts. The wedge is one maize or coffee cooperative with one insurer.
why_now: Local crop datasets and small on-device models exist now, and FarmerChat has answered 8M+ farmer questions, so farmers already talk to AI on their phones.
revenue_model: $0.50-2 per policy per season for verification, or a share of premium.
non_obvious_insight: Basis risk is solved by dense ground truth from the insured themselves, not by better satellites.
first_30_days: Partner with a cooperative of about 2,000 farmers and run photo verification in parallel with existing claims for one season.

title: Supervised-Hours Bench for Counselors and Social Workers
one_liner: A managed group-supervision network and hour-logging platform that lets clinics fund the thousands of post-degree supervised hours gating counseling, MFT and social-work licenses.
customer: Group therapy practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts hiring associate-level counselors and social workers; the associates themselves.
problem: Counseling, psychology and social work were excluded from the higher federal loan cap. Licensure typically requires 2-4k supervised hours after the degree, and associates often pay $50-150 an hour out of pocket for supervision that is scarce and tracked on paper. Clinics cannot hire associates faster than supervisors can be found.
solution: Certified supervisors, often semi-retired licensed clinicians, deliver state-compliant group supervision by video. The platform logs hours in board-ready format and enforces state ratios and rules. Clinics pay per associate per month to onboard associates who can bill insurance under supervision.
why_now: The July 2026 loan caps squeeze students in excluded fields and push them toward employer support. Behavioral-health demand is high, and telesupervision is widely permitted in many states after the pandemic.
revenue_model: $150-300 per associate per month from the clinic, supervision delivery margin, and hour-logging SaaS. Optional share of billed associate revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in the credential chain is not the degree but post-degree supervision, and the payer is the employer, not the student, because associates bill insurance and become revenue-positive once supervised.
first_30_days: Pick one large state that permits telesupervision. Recruit 5 licensed supervisors. Sign 3 group practices with about 10 associates in total. Run the hour logs in spreadsheets first and charge $200 per associate per month. Verify board rules before selling.

title: Pooled Radiation Test Data for Commercial Chips
one_liner: A subscription database and beam-time broker so satellite builders stop each paying to test the same commercial chips.
customer: Constellation and smallsat builders using commercial parts, defense new-space suppliers, and chip vendors seeking space design wins.
problem: Proliferated constellations (Golden Dome's reported 600-satellite award, Starlink) run on commercial parts. Radiation-beam slots are scarce with multi-month queues, and results live in silos. Roughly the same popular parts get tested repeatedly.
solution: Pool member orders to buy block beam time at university and national facilities, and test the top parts by lot and date code. Publish a member-contributed database of results and anomalies, and broker custom tests. Members trade their data for access.
why_now: Defense demand for proliferated LEO and a wave of well-funded satellite makers are stressing limited test capacity. Commercial-parts-first design is now standard.
revenue_model: $10-50k per year per member. 10-15% fee on brokered custom tests. Sponsored testing from chip vendors.
non_obvious_insight: In a commercial-parts space industry, test data is the scarce asset, not the parts. The group that pools it becomes the standards-setter.
first_30_days: Contact two beam facilities about block-time pricing. Pre-sell five founding memberships to satellite builders at $10k each. Publish a free first report on one popular microcontroller or memory part to establish credibility.

title: Celebration-of-Life Halls in Closed Churches
one_liner: Lease shuttered churches and run them as turnkey memorial venues sold at checkout by direct-cremation providers and hospices.
customer: Families holding a memorial after a cremation ($2.5-6k per event). Referral partners are low-cost and direct-cremation providers, hospice social workers and estate attorneys.
problem: Cremation was about 62% of US dispositions in 2024 and is projected to hit ~82% by 2045. Direct cremation is the fastest-growing category, but it unbundles the ceremony. Families end up planning a memorial themselves in a restaurant or backyard, funeral-home chapels are being sold off, and nobody runs the day: music, slideshow, live-stream, seating, catering, display of ashes.
solution: Take a long lease or lease-to-own on a closed church. Denominations often discount buildings for gentle uses and restrict bars or clubs, so a memorial hall is an easy yes. Install AV and live-streaming for far-away family, and hire a bereavement-trained coordinator. Add a photo-to-memorial-video service, caterer partnerships and a wall of memory. Sell it as a $2,900 'Add a Celebration of Life' package on the partner's checkout page. The other six days a week, book weddings, concerts and community events. Columbarium niches are a phase-two option after legal review.
why_now: Direct-cremation startups have marketing reach and no physical venues. Congregations keep closing after COVID. Live-stream AV and AI-assisted photo-to-video tools are now cheap enough for a two-person team to run.
revenue_model: Event package fee (venue, AV, coordinator; $2.5-6k). Catering margin. Memorial video upsell (~$400). Referral revenue share to partners. Weekday event rentals. Later, columbarium niches with perpetual-care fees.
non_obvious_insight: The direct-cremation revolution unbundled the ceremony and nobody rebundled it. A sanctuary already has the emotional weight and acoustics, and resale restrictions make sellers accept a low price for a respectful use. Idle-week rental income turns a grief business into a resilient one.
first_30_days: Contact diocesan and conference property offices about 5 closed churches for month-to-month special-use agreements. Pilot 3 events at cost-plus with 2 direct-cremation providers and 2 hospices. Collect testimonials and photos. Stand up a booking page and a bereavement-friendly phone concierge.

title: Contest-Proof Signing: Capacity Sessions for Wills
one_liner: A recorded, clinician-run capacity and intent session at will signing, so a later contest by disappointed heirs has strong evidence against it.
customer: Estate-planning and elder-law attorneys and RIAs whose clients are 75+, in blended families or making unequal bequests. Clients pay the clinical entity directly, and firms bundle it into fixed-fee packages.
problem: An older wealthy cohort, more second marriages and rising dementia diagnoses mean more disputes about capacity and undue influence. Evidence of capacity at signing is usually the drafting lawyer's memory plus boilerplate. That is weak in court and expensive to defend.
solution: A standardized signing-day product. A licensed geriatric psychiatrist or neuropsychologist runs a structured, recorded interview with validated screening, an independent private conversation without family, and a recorded 'why I chose this' statement. The bundle is hashed and stored under the attorney's privilege, with an optional yearly refresh and in-home or remote delivery.
why_now: FDA cleared blood tests for Alzheimer's pathology in 2025, so more people get an early diagnosis and want to sign while they still can. Remote notarization and e-will laws widened access, and video is cheap. The transfer is concentrated in older households with complex families.
revenue_model: $700-$1,500 per session billed by the clinical entity, firm-level packages of $25K/year, and yearly refresh sessions. Lawyer referral-fee rules make direct client billing the safer structure (check state ethics rules).
non_obvious_insight: Capacity is a moment-in-time question and the evidence is manufactured at the signing. It is cheap to create then and impossible to recreate later. Diagnosis awareness is creating a rush window nobody is serving.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 geriatric psychiatrists or neuropsychologists per metro. Partner with 5 elder-law firms. Run 20 sessions at $900 and have each firm's litigators review the artifact bundle. Keep clean records of what each session found.
